basis: God supplies an infant through the mother's breasts
note: Augustine thanks God for providing infant food through the mother's breasts rather than treating maternal nursing as self-sufficient. This Christian reading closely parallels the commentary's distinction between the visible mother and the true divine guardian of a child's nurture.

basis: virgin's womb holds the Provider as an infant
note: Ephrem's Nativity hymn dwells on the paradox that the Provider enters the Virgin's womb and accepts infant need. It is a Syriac Christian theological rereading of womb as dwelling and nurture; stanza numbering varies across editions.

basis: God creates humans to grow toward perfection
note: Irenaeus argues that created humanity must grow gradually toward perfection rather than receive its final capacity all at once. This patristic account gives a theological analogue to the commentary's definition of terbiye as movement through states to completion.

basis: painless virginal delivery in a Christian hymn
note: The ode's birth image is commonly read as portraying the Virgin's delivery without pain. Against the commentary's laboring maternal body, it offers a specifically Christian theological reversal rather than a shared account; the ode's transmission and verse division warrant caution.

basis: Syriac r-ḥ-m mercy vocabulary
note: The commentary labels Arabic ر ح م as the root of mercy; the Syriac Peshitta uses the cognate r-ḥ-m word family for God’s mercies in this verse, where mercy brings the dawn to those in darkness.

basis: Mary's childhood nourishment in the temple
note: In the common chapter division, three-year-old Mary is placed at the temple and receives food from an angel. This infancy tradition adds a distinctly Christian scene of a child reared outside her parents' home; chapter and verse divisions vary by translation.

basis: Joseph assigned as Mary's guardian
note: In the usual chapter division, the priests assign the older Joseph to keep Mary when she can no longer remain in the temple. This infancy tradition extends the commentary's nonbirth-caregiver question into a Christian guardianship narrative; details and chapter subdivision vary by translation.

basis: leaving childhood ways for adulthood
note: Paul uses the passage from child to adult as the figure for a completed mode of knowing. It is a brief but exact New Testament staging of maturation that belongs beside terbiye's movement toward completion.

basis: teacher feeds learners milk
note: The commentary calls a teacher one who feeds people small portions of knowledge; Paul says he fed the Corinthians milk rather than solid food because they were not ready for it.

basis: teacher gives milk before solid food
note: Paul says he gave the Corinthians milk rather than solid food because they were not ready. It is the clearest New Testament analogue to the commentary's teacher who nourishes people first with small portions of knowledge.

basis: spiritual fatherhood exceeds guardianship
note: Paul contrasts many guardians in Christ with his singular fatherhood through the gospel. It gives a particularly close Christian distinction between a supervising caregiver and a formative parent, matching the commentary's careful nonbirth-parent vocabulary.

basis: compassion must become help
note: The commentary defines mercy as tenderness that requires beneficence toward its object, especially the weak; John asks how God’s love can remain in someone who closes his inward compassion to a brother in need.

basis: compassion proved by material help
note: One who sees a sibling in need and closes the inward organs of compassion is challenged to show God's love. The verse makes compassion concrete through goods and need, matching the commentary's insistence that mercy entails beneficent action.

basis: newborns grow on milk
note: The commentary’s child grows through successive stages under nurture; Peter urges newborn infants to long for pure spiritual milk so they may grow into salvation.

basis: newborns crave milk in order to grow
note: Newborn infants are urged to desire pure spiritual milk so that they may grow toward salvation. The verse makes milk, infancy, teaching, and purposeful maturation one integrated image.

basis: a father addresses his children
note: The commentary pairs the mother’s womb and a father’s role in raising a child; Paul recalls exhorting and encouraging each Thessalonian as a father addresses his own children.

basis: father exhorts, encourages, and comforts children
note: Paul also compares his work to a father dealing with each child through exhortation, encouragement, and consolation. Together with maternal nursing in the preceding image, it makes cultivation a patient parental practice.

basis: parental guidance toward a worthy life
note: The commentary says upbringing leads step by step toward completion; Paul says he urged the community to live worthily of God, like a father guiding children toward their calling.

basis: nursing mother’s tenderness
note: The commentary’s rahma is tenderness expressed as care and its Rab image is nurturing; Paul says he was gentle among the Thessalonians like a nursing mother cherishing her own children.

basis: nursing mother cherishes her own children
note: Paul depicts his gentle pastoral care as a nursing mother cherishing her children. The image links bodily nurture and nonbiological teaching care in precisely the double register developed by the commentary.

basis: sharing life with those nurtured
note: The commentary describes care as more than a feeling, extending to an actual good for the cared-for; Paul says he shared not only the gospel but his own life with the community because they had become dear to him.

basis: managing one's household and caring for God's assembly
note: The argument reasons from managing one's own household to caring for God's church. It is a direct Christian development of the commentary's claim that standing up a household's affairs is a genuine form of care.

basis: children repay care at home
note: The commentary links mercy toward parents to their raising the child while small; Paul says descendants should learn to show piety at home and make some return to their parents and grandparents.

basis: children repay parents through care for their household
note: Children and grandchildren must first practice piety toward their own household and make return to their parents. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's Qur'an 17:23–24 reversal from parental raising to a child's merciful responsibility.

basis: provide for one’s household
note: The commentary’s household upholder supplies and protects the family; Paul says providing for one’s own household is a concrete family duty and failure repudiates the faith.

basis: parents store up for children
note: Paul invokes the household norm that parents should save for children, not children for parents. It directly connects parenthood with provision, complementing the commentary's domestic food and child-rearing images.

basis: Sacred writings known from infancy
note: Timothy has known the sacred writings from infancy, which can make him wise for salvation. It is a direct image of instruction beginning in childhood and reaching mature discernment.

basis: Moses nurtured in his father's house
note: Stephen says Moses was brought up for three months in his father's house. The retelling explicitly foregrounds the protected natal home before exposure, which the commentary contrasts with later palace claims.

basis: Moses adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter
note: The commentary recounts Moses’ exposure and return to his mother; Stephen recalls Pharaoh’s daughter taking and raising him as her own son, a Christian retelling that foregrounds the adoptive household.

basis: Pharaoh's daughter raises Moses as son
note: Acts says that Pharaoh's daughter took up the exposed Moses and raised him as her own son. It preserves the foster-child transition central to the commentary's distinction between birth, nursing, and a later household's nurture.

basis: Moses educated in the palace
note: The commentary calls Pharaoh’s “we raised you” only a partial claim; Stephen says Moses was instructed in all Egyptian wisdom and was powerful in words and deeds, preserving palace education alongside the commentary’s emphasis on his mother and God.

basis: Moses instructed in Egyptian wisdom
note: Stephen says Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and became powerful in words and deeds. It supplies the educational continuation of the foster-household narrative, relevant to the commentary's move from being raised to being taught.

basis: parents must not crush children
note: The commentary presents raising a child as beneficial formation toward completion; Colossians warns fathers not to embitter children lest they lose heart, marking a limit on parental authority.

basis: growth toward mature fullness
note: The community is to reach mature adulthood and the measure of Christ's full stature. This provides an explicit Christian endpoint for the commentary's halden hale movement to the limit of completion.

basis: nourishing and cherishing one’s own
note: The commentary describes a home that nurtures and protects its members; Ephesians says no one hates his own body but nourishes and cherishes it, then uses that care to explain Christ’s care for the church.

basis: nourishing and cherishing as embodied care
note: A person nourishes and cherishes his own body, as Christ does the church. The verb for nourishing extends the commentary's rearing imagery into a Christian account of sustained, intimate care.

basis: children obey parents
note: The commentary’s parent-child frame moves from receiving nurture to responding to parents; Ephesians addresses children directly and commands obedience in the Lord.

basis: children honor father and mother
note: The commentary pairs worship of God with doing good to parents who raised the child; Ephesians repeats the command to honor father and mother, grounding filial duty in the commandment.

basis: parents raise children toward maturity
note: The commentary defines Rab as raising a child toward completion; Ephesians tells fathers to bring children up in the Lord’s discipline and instruction, placing education inside parental care.

basis: bring children up in instruction of the Lord
note: Fathers are told to bring children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord rather than embitter them. It directly connects household upbringing, moral formation, and teaching.

basis: formation through labor
note: The commentary’s womb image and staged raising meet Paul’s labor metaphor: he is again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in his converts.

basis: maternal labor until Christ is formed in learners
note: Paul likens his pastoral work to being in labor until Christ is formed in his children. It turns the commentary's womb, labor, and gradual formation into an explicitly pedagogical Christian metaphor.

basis: child placed under guardians and household managers
note: The heir, while a child, is under guardians and managers until the father's appointed time. This is a particularly exact legal and domestic analogue for the commentary's nonbirth caregiver and the person who maintains a household's affairs.

basis: God's son born of a woman
note: God sends his Son, born of a woman and under the law. The verse keeps incarnation within a concrete maternal birth while the surrounding argument moves toward adoption, furnishing both sides of the commentary's womb and foster-family frame.

basis: adoption into God’s family
note: The commentary notes a spouse raising a child who is not biologically theirs; Paul says Christ redeems those under the law so they may receive adoption as children, applying household adoption to believers.

basis: Moses refuses Pharaoh’s daughter’s sonship
note: The commentary calls Pharaoh’s claim to have raised Moses only partial; Hebrews says Moses, when grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, making royal upbringing distinct from the identity he chose.

basis: discipline yields trained righteousness
note: Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it. Its temporal account of costly formation is a close conceptual partner to terbiye as gradual maturation.

basis: straight paths heal what is weak
note: After the discipline argument, hearers are told to make straight paths for their feet so that what is lame may be healed. It links the commentary's straight path to formative care for the weak rather than to direction alone.

basis: fatherly discipline addressed to a son
note: The exhortation cites the address, "My son," and tells the child not to reject the Lord's discipline. This supplies the explicit father-son language whose later training result appears in Heb. 12:11.

basis: Christian reading of Proverbs’ fatherly discipline
note: The commentary describes nurture as formation toward completion; Hebrews quotes the father-son discipline saying from Proverbs and interprets hardship as the Lord’s treatment of children he receives, giving correction a filial meaning.

basis: milk and solid food mark learning stages
note: The commentary defines upbringing as moving from state to state toward completion; Hebrews rebukes hearers who still need milk rather than solid food when they should be teachers.

basis: milk and elementary instruction before mature teaching
note: The readers, who should be teachers, need the elementary words again and have become people needing milk. It adds the pedagogical problem behind the commentary's image of feeding learners small pieces of knowledge.

basis: maturity follows training
note: The commentary’s education image moves toward completion; Hebrews says solid food belongs to the mature, whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil.

basis: solid food belongs to the mature
note: Maturity is marked by solid food and trained powers of discernment. It completes the milk-to-maturity progression that the commentary's small portions of knowledge and final completion invite readers to trace.

basis: compassion fails without food and clothing
note: James rejects telling an inadequately clothed and hungry sibling to depart in peace without giving what the body needs. It makes the commentary's mercy-to-beneficence claim a sharply practical test involving household necessities.

basis: birth from God rather than blood or human will
note: The prologue describes those born not from blood, fleshly will, or a man's will, but from God. It offers a Johannine redescription of descent that stands in productive tension with the commentary's bodily womb and kinship account.

basis: source ر ب ب: ῥαββί glossed as Teacher
note: John preserves the Semitic address ῥαββί and immediately glosses it as Teacher. As an actual r-b-b cognate, it substantiates the commentary's carefully developed extension from Rabb to a teacher rather than relying on the root label alone.

basis: labor pain and joy after birth
note: The commentary recalls pain in the womb after delivery; Jesus compares grief followed by joy to a woman distressed in labor who rejoices after her child is born, preserving the passage’s focus on labor and birth rather than postpartum illness.

basis: birth pain gives way to joy at the child's arrival
note: Jesus uses a woman in labor whose anguish turns to joy when a human being is born. It directly meets the commentary's emphasis on the bodily cost of birth, while assigning that image an eschatological meaning.

basis: new family formed at the cross
note: The commentary describes kinship through a shared womb and care within a household; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, forming a caregiving family relation not based on common birth.

basis: the disciple takes Mary into his home
note: The commentary describes kinship through a shared womb and care within a household; after entrusting his mother to the disciple, Jesus’ words lead the disciple to take her into his own home, making protection concrete.

basis: a chosen disciple takes Jesus' mother into his home
note: Jesus establishes a new mother-son relation, and the disciple takes her into his own household. This is a concrete Christian scene of nonbiological family care that belongs beside the commentary's step-parent and child-minder images.

basis: Aramaic Rabbouni / teacher
note: The commentary labels Arabic ر ب ب as the root behind “Rab” and associates it with raising and teaching; Mary addresses Jesus as Rabbouni, “my teacher,” in the scene where she recognizes him after the resurrection.

basis: returning to the mother's womb questioned
note: Nicodemus asks whether an adult can enter a mother's womb a second time and be born. The question makes physical womb-life explicit, while the ensuing Johannine discourse redirects birth to a different, Spirit-centered register rather than the commentary's original womb-house.

basis: all will be taught by God
note: Jesus cites the promise that all will be taught by God. The direct divine-teacher formulation is a New Testament companion to the commentary's Rahman who teaches the Qur'an and teaches human expression.

basis: an infant responds within the mother's womb
note: At Mary's greeting, the infant leaps in Elizabeth's womb and she is filled with the Holy Spirit. The scene gives the womb a responsive sacred interior, alongside the commentary's womb as a divinely active place of formation.

basis: a child moves in the womb
note: The commentary’s central image is the womb as the child’s home; Elizabeth says the child in her womb leapt when Mary’s greeting reached her, a specific intrauterine scene.

basis: visceral mercy
note: The commentary links Arabic raḥma to the womb and defines it as tender feeling that issues in care; Luke describes God’s mercy with the Greek word for inward parts, making divine compassion bodily and generative in the dawn song.

basis: tenderness toward a wounded stranger
note: The commentary says mercy is a tenderness that leads to good action for the weak; the Samaritan sees an injured outsider and is moved with compassion, turning feeling into care.

basis: care becomes practical shelter
note: The commentary ties mercy to household care and provision; the Samaritan binds the wounded man, puts him on his animal, and takes him to an inn, supplying a temporary home for the vulnerable.

basis: womb and breasts named as maternal blessing
note: The commentary explicitly develops the womb, the child’s home, and the nurturing relation; a woman blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts that nursed him.

basis: womb and breasts praised for bearing and nursing Jesus
note: A woman blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts he nursed. This is an unusually explicit New Testament meeting with the commentary's womb-as-home and maternal-nourishment language.

basis: Jesus redirects blessing to hearing the word
note: The commentary connects maternal nurture with the teacher who feeds learners; Jesus answers the womb-and-breast blessing by calling blessed those who hear God’s word and keep it, shifting the measure toward instruction and response.

basis: blessedness redirected to hearing and keeping God's word
note: Jesus answers the blessing of womb and breasts by pronouncing blessed those who hear and keep God's word. The response does not erase the preceding maternal image, but redirects its privileged meaning toward received teaching, a contrast central to the commentary's womb-to-learning movement.

basis: faithful manager supplies food at the proper time
note: Jesus' faithful household manager gives the servants their food allowance at the proper time. This joins the commentary's qawwam-like keeper of household affairs with its secondary image of food provision and measured nurture.

basis: a protective mother gathers children
note: The commentary joins the household’s protection to the image of a vulnerable child; Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, but they are unwilling.

basis: a father receives his child with compassion
note: The commentary places mercy around the image of a child growing under parental care; the father sees his returning son, is moved with compassion, runs to him, embraces and kisses him, restoring a broken household bond.

basis: Jesus grows, becomes strong, and is filled with wisdom
note: The infancy narrative describes Jesus' growth, strengthening, wisdom, and divine favor. It gives a canonical Christian rendering of child development in stages rather than a single moment of birth.

basis: Jesus grows in wisdom and favor
note: The commentary describes upbringing as carrying a child from one state to completion; Luke reports Jesus growing in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and people.

basis: Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and favor
note: Jesus continues to advance in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and people. Its triadic maturation closely fits the commentary's movement from a child's home through cultivation toward completion.

basis: merciful as the Father is merciful
note: Jesus grounds merciful action in the Father's mercy. This provides a father-child divine frame for the commentary's claim that rahma is tenderness that becomes beneficence toward others.

basis: compassion for a bereaved mother
note: The commentary says mercy bends toward the weak and recounts a mother’s separation from Moses; Jesus is moved with compassion for a widow whose only son is being carried out, a distinct mother-and-son scene.

basis: compassion for a bereaved mother and her only son
note: Jesus sees the bereaved widow and is moved with compassion before addressing her loss. The scene places mercy beside a mother's emptied household and anticipates restoration of her child, close to the commentary's maternal grief and return motif.

basis: the son returned to his mother
note: The commentary recounts Moses being returned to his mother; Jesus restores the widow’s son to life and gives him back to her, so the shared detail is reunion, though Luke’s son is grown and the event is a resurrection.

basis: Jesus takes children in his arms
note: The commentary says mercy especially bends toward the weak; Jesus takes little children in his arms, lays hands on them, and blesses them after the disciples tried to keep them away.

basis: kinship beyond one womb
note: The commentary explains “rahim” as kin related because they came from one womb; Jesus calls those who do God’s will his brother, sister, and mother, extending family relation beyond biological birth.

basis: religion cannot cancel parental care
note: The commentary says children owe good and mercy to the parents who raised them; Jesus condemns a dedication formula that lets a person withhold material support from father or mother.

basis: the Father's will that no little one perish
note: Jesus states that the heavenly Father does not will the loss of even one little one. It is a precise divine-parental articulation of mercy toward the weak child.

basis: mother bird gathers young under her wings
note: Jesus compares his desired protection of Jerusalem's children to a hen gathering her brood under her wings. The maternal protective figure supplies a New Testament meeting with the commentary's mercy, weak young, and guarded household.

basis: parents give good gifts to children
note: The commentary joins mercy with doing good and the Lord with a child’s nurturer; Jesus argues from human parents giving good gifts to their children toward the heavenly Father’s greater generosity.

basis: father gives good things to children
note: Human parents' giving of good gifts becomes the measure for the heavenly Father's generosity. It joins parental provision and divine goodness, illuminating the commentary's en'amte image of children being reared in ease.

basis: adoption and the cry Abba, Father
note: The Spirit of adoption enables believers to cry, "Abba, Father." This makes nonbiological incorporation into a parental divine household an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's birth-parent and foster-parent distinctions.

basis: grace appears for all
note: The commentary joins the merciful Lord with formation; Titus says God’s saving grace has appeared for all people, setting the context for grace’s ethical training in the next verse.

basis: grace trains people to live well
note: The commentary describes nurture as gradual formation toward completion; Titus says grace trains people to renounce ungodliness and live with self-control, righteousness, and devotion.

basis: mother credits the Creator with her children's life
note: The martyred brothers' mother says she does not know how they came to be in her womb and attributes life, breath, and bodily formation to the Creator. It directly combines maternal gestation with divine formative agency.

basis: teachers for children
note: The commentary describes a teacher feeding people small portions of knowledge; the tradition about Joshua ben Gamla establishes teachers for children in towns, turning that nourishment into an institution.

basis: father’s concrete duties to a son
note: The commentary’s Rab raises and teaches a child; Kiddushin lists a father’s obligations to his son, including teaching Torah and a trade, making nurture a set of practical responsibilities.

basis: Torah taught in the womb
note: The commentary calls the womb a child’s home and pairs it with teaching toward completion; Niddah imagines a fetus taught the whole Torah in the womb, then made to forget it at birth.

basis: communal teachers for children
note: The account of Joshua ben Gamla's school reform makes accessible teachers for children a communal duty. It develops the commentary's teacher-nurturer image into an institutional form of care for learners who cannot yet sustain themselves.

basis: parental duties of bodily, Torah, and vocational formation
note: The Bavli enumerates a father's obligations toward a son, including circumcision, redemption, Torah instruction, marriage, and a trade. It gives a concrete rabbinic map of upbringing that moves beyond birth toward a child's completed social and religious formation.

basis: stages of learning and adulthood
note: The commentary’s teacher feeds learners small portions of knowledge and its upbringing proceeds in stages to completion; Avot gives successive ages for Scripture, Mishnah, commandments, study, marriage, and adult responsibility.

basis: ordered ages for Scripture, Mishnah, commandments, and maturity
note: Avot's age sequence makes learning and responsibility unfold in stages. It supplies a rabbinic analogue to the commentary's definition of terbiye as bringing a thing state by state to completion.

basis: fetus taught Torah in the womb
note: The Bavli imagines an angel teaching the fetus the whole Torah in the womb before birth. This is an interpretive, not narrative, parallel that fuses the commentary's womb-house with its later claim that nurture reaches teaching.

basis: father, mother, and God as partners in a child's formation
note: The Bavli divides a child's making among father, mother, and the Holy One. Its three-agent account offers a Jewish interpretive framework for the commentary's distinction between maternal body, human caregivers, and the divine shaper.

basis: care for an aging father
note: The commentary says children should respond with mercy to parents who raised them when they were small; Sirach instructs a child to help the father in old age and not grieve him.

basis: honor and help a father in old age
note: Ben Sira tells a child to help rather than grieve a father in old age. This places the grown child's mercy and practical care toward parents beside the commentary's Qur'an 17:23–24 reversal of the earlier raising relationship.

basis: patience when a parent declines
note: The commentary’s filial image includes lowering oneself in mercy before parents; Sirach tells the child to be patient if the father’s mind fails and not to despise him in the child’s own strength.

basis: kindness to parents remembered
note: The commentary grounds care of parents in their earlier nurturing; Sirach says kindness to a father will not be forgotten and will count against sins.

basis: Moses refuses Egyptian wet nurses
note: The Bavli expands Exodus 2 by making Moses refuse Egyptian nurses until his own mother feeds him, because his mouth is destined for divine speech. That interpretation intensifies the commentary's claim that his true nurture occurs at his mother's breast under God's care.

basis: God retains the key of childbirth
note: The Bavli lists childbirth among the keys that God does not entrust to an intermediary, grounding it in Rachel's opened womb. This is a direct Jewish interpretive assertion of the divine agency behind the commentary's womb and birth images.

basis: remember the dangers endured in the womb
note: Tobit tells his son to remember the many dangers his mother underwent for him in her womb. It is a close Jewish counterpart to the commentary's refusal to sentimentalize the womb-house or detach filial duty from maternal cost.

basis: Elijah returns a son to his mother
note: The commentary recounts Moses being restored to his mother after separation; Elijah brings the widow’s revived son down and gives him to her, a distinct Hebrew Bible reunion scene.

basis: raḥamim / maternal compassion
note: The commentary’s Arabic womb-and-mercy root has a Hebrew cognate here: the living child’s mother’s raḥamim “stir” and she yields her claim to save him, making compassion protective action for a vulnerable child.

basis: mother protects the weak child
note: The commentary defines mercy as tenderness that leads to beneficence, especially toward the weak; the true mother gives up her claim rather than let the infant be cut in two.

basis: source ر ح م: maternal רחמים acts to save a son
note: The true mother's compassion, Hebrew rahamim, is stirred for her son and she yields him rather than see him killed. This is not merely emotion: it performs the commentary's definition of rahma as tenderness that entails beneficent action toward the weak.

basis: Hannah nurses until weaning
note: The commentary makes growth in a womb and later nurturing part of one child’s story; Hannah keeps Samuel with her until he is weaned before bringing him to serve at Shiloh.

basis: weaning marks a new stage
note: The commentary describes bringing a child state by state toward completion; after Samuel is weaned, Hannah brings him to the sanctuary with provisions, marking a transition from maternal nursing to another form of service and care.

basis: Hannah continues to provide after weaning
note: The commentary treats nurturing as continuing beyond birth and recognizes care by someone outside the child’s daily home; although Samuel serves at Shiloh, his mother brings him a small robe each year.

basis: Samuel grows in stature and favor
note: The child Samuel continues to grow in stature and in favor with YHWH and people. It is a concise biblical sequence from protected childhood toward mature, socially and divinely recognized formation.

basis: child and nurse hidden from royal violence
note: Jehosheba takes the infant Joash with his nurse and hides them in a bedroom from those killing royal children. This is a separate biblical child-preservation scene joining danger, a nurse, concealment, and a substitute household.

basis: ewe lamb raised in the home
note: The commentary records the dictionary gloss of a rubbā ewe kept in the house for milk; Nathan’s ewe lamb eats from the poor man’s morsel, drinks from his cup, lies in his bosom, and is “like a daughter.”

basis: lamb grows inside the household as a daughter
note: Nathan's poor man's lamb grows up with him and his children, shares food and drink, lies in his bosom, and is like a daughter. It makes the commentary's domestic sheep image into a striking household scene of nurtured dependence.

basis: source ق و م: Hebrew הקים, raising and establishing a descendant
note: God promises David that he will raise up his offspring after him and establish his kingdom. Hebrew q-w-m is a real cognate field for the commentary's qawwam, but this verse shifts from daily household support to securing a child and dynasty.

basis: God as father who disciplines a son
note: God promises of David's heir, "I will be his father and he will be my son," and speaks of correction when he errs. This is a direct biblical parent-child account of lordly formation that includes discipline as well as care.

basis: God carries Israel as a father carries a son
note: The commentary moves from the womb to a child raised by a household; Moses recalls God carrying Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son, a direct parental-care image.

basis: God carries Israel as a parent carries a child
note: Moses recalls YHWH carrying Israel in the wilderness as a man carries his son. It makes the divine Lord a sustaining parent across a journey, not simply a begetter, matching the commentary's transition from womb to ongoing rabbi-like cultivation.

basis: food and clothing for the fatherless and widow
note: The commentary defines mercy as doing good to the weak and mentions household provision; Deuteronomy says God upholds the orphan and widow and gives the resident alien food and clothing.

basis: God feeds and clothes the vulnerable outsider
note: God executes justice for orphan and widow and loves the resident alien by giving food and clothing. It offers a concrete biblical form of the commentary's mercy that bends toward the weak and becomes provision.

basis: God guards Israel as the apple of his eye
note: The wilderness song says that God found, encircled, cared for, and guarded Israel as the apple of his eye. This is a close biblical companion to Musa being brought up under God's eye rather than merely under Pharaoh's claim.

basis: eagle carries its young
note: The commentary pictures a child’s home as protected while it is brought toward maturity; Moses’ song depicts God as an eagle stirring its nest, spreading wings, catching and carrying its young.

basis: a parent bird trains and carries its young
note: The eagle stirs its nest, hovers over its young, spreads wings, takes them, and bears them. Its patient sequence of urging, sheltering, and carrying gives a vivid animal analogue to terbiye as growth through successive states.

basis: God who gave birth is forgotten
note: The commentary surrounds nurture with womb and parental care; Moses’ song accuses Israel of forgetting the Rock who gave birth to them, reversing the expected child’s response to the one who formed and raised them.

basis: one Lord and the household’s teaching
note: The commentary says the Fatiha’s exclusive worship and its “Lord” meet the duty of family care; Deuteronomy places Israel’s confession of one Lord immediately before commands to love God and teach the words to children.

basis: teaching children through daily life
note: The commentary’s teacher nurtures learners in small stages; Deuteronomy requires parents to teach children at home, on the road, at bedtime, and on rising, making instruction continuous and domestic.

basis: teach the words diligently to children at home
note: Israel is commanded to teach the words to children while sitting at home, walking, lying down, and rising. This supplies a concrete domestic rhythm for the commentary's claim that upbringing extends into instruction.

basis: food and instruction in the wilderness
note: The commentary joins the household’s feeding with a teacher’s gradual nourishment of learners; Deuteronomy says God let Israel hunger, fed them manna, and taught that life depends on God’s word.

basis: God disciplines as a father
note: The commentary defines “Rab” as raising a child toward completion; Moses says God disciplines Israel as a man disciplines his son, interpreting wilderness hardship as parental formation.

basis: divine discipline as a father disciplines a son
note: Israel is to recognize that YHWH disciplines it as a man disciplines his son. This gives a biblical parent-child account of formative correction, a necessary complication and parallel to terbiye as gradual movement toward completion.

basis: God's work hidden in a pregnant womb
note: Qoheleth compares the unknowable work of God with not knowing how bones develop in a pregnant woman's womb. The comparison makes prenatal formation an arena of divine hiddenness, complementing the commentary's more affirmative image of God shaping there.

basis: Mordecai raises Esther
note: The commentary includes a step-parent or guardian who takes responsibility for a child’s upbringing; Esther says Mordecai raised her as his own daughter after her parents died.

basis: Mordecai brings up an orphan as his daughter
note: Mordecai raises Hadassah after the death of her parents and takes her as his own daughter. It is a concrete household instance of the commentary's claim that raising a child can belong to someone other than the one who gave birth.

basis: Pharaoh orders sons cast into the Nile
note: Pharaoh commands that every Hebrew son be thrown into the Nile. This supplies the lethal political setting that makes Moses' mother's water placement in the commentary a protective counter-use of the same water.

basis: palace adoption
note: The commentary calls Pharaoh’s “did we not raise you?” only a partial claim and ends with Moses restored to his mother; Exodus says Pharaoh’s daughter adopts him as her son and names him Moses.

basis: Pharaoh's daughter adopts Moses
note: After he grows, Moses becomes Pharaoh's daughter's son. This makes Qur'an 26:18's collective claim that Pharaoh's household raised Musa a pointedly different household claim: the biblical named foster parent is the daughter, not Pharaoh as speaker.

basis: Moses hidden before being sent onto the river
note: The commentary’s Qur’anic account begins with God directing Moses’ mother to nurse him and then place him in the water; Exodus first says she hides the newborn for three months, a distinct step before the basket episode.

basis: mother bears, sees, and hides Moses
note: Moses' mother gives birth, sees that he is good, and hides him for three months. This verse supplies the maternal fear and prior home-care that precede the basket scene and the commentary's nursing mother.

basis: Moses in the basket
note: The commentary recounts Moses’ mother placing him in the river and his later return; Exodus gives the same endangered-child scene, with the basket among the reeds on the Nile.

basis: Musa's mother, nursing child, water separation
note: When Moses' mother can no longer conceal him, she puts him in a waterproof basket among the Nile reeds. It is the concrete biblical water-separation scene beside the commentary's mother who nurses Musa and sends him into the yamm; Exodus supplies concealment as the immediate motive.

basis: Musa's sister watches from afar
note: Moses' sister stations herself to learn what will happen to him. This is the narrative counterpart to the sister who identifies a household able to foster Musa in the commentary.

basis: Pharaoh’s daughter finds the infant
note: The commentary says the Pharaoh household takes Moses but emphasizes the sister’s proposal and his return to his mother; Exodus identifies Pharaoh’s daughter as the one who finds the basket and sends her servant to fetch it.

basis: compassion for an exposed child
note: The commentary says mercy turns tenderness toward the weak into good action; Pharaoh’s daughter sees the crying Hebrew infant and pities him, prompting protection inside the palace household.

basis: mercy for the crying, exposed child
note: Pharaoh's daughter opens the basket, sees the crying child, and has compassion. Her response makes the commentary's claim that mercy turns toward the weak into the act that begins Moses' rescue.

basis: sister finds a nurse
note: The commentary says Moses’ sister proposes a household to rear him and that he is returned to his mother; Exodus has the sister offer to find a Hebrew wet nurse, so the birth mother becomes his paid nurse rather than a proposed foster household.

basis: sister proposes a nursing household
note: The sister offers to call a Hebrew woman to nurse the child. The same child-sister-household nexus underlies Qur'an 28:12's offer of an ahl bayt who will care for him, though Exodus specifies a wet nurse.

basis: mother takes Moses to nurse him
note: The commentary’s version returns Moses to his mother after the sister’s intervention; Exodus likewise reunites them, but Pharaoh’s daughter sends the girl to fetch the mother, who nurses him in her own home.

basis: paid maternal nursing
note: The commentary makes the mother’s breast and God’s oversight the real nurture behind Pharaoh’s later claim; Exodus explicitly has Pharaoh’s daughter pay the birth mother to nurse the child.

basis: mother is returned as paid nurse
note: Pharaoh's daughter entrusts the child to his own mother to nurse and pays her. It is the close biblical counterpart to Musa's return to his mother, joining maternal breast, a nonmaternal household, and providential restoration.

basis: honor for father and mother
note: The commentary makes mercy to parents a response to their raising a child while small; the command to honor father and mother supplies the corresponding Hebrew Bible duty, with long life in the land as its stated consequence.

basis: r-ḥ-m / raḥum
note: The commentary labels Arabic ر ح م as the source root for mercy; Hebrew raḥum is a cognate used in YHWH’s self-description after the calf episode, where compassion is joined to patience and covenant fidelity.

basis: Israel as God's firstborn son
note: God calls Israel his firstborn son in the message to Pharaoh. This makes divine lordship a parental relation and gives political force to the commentary's account of the Rabb who nurtures children.

basis: an abandoned newborn lacks ordinary care
note: Jerusalem is figured as a newborn whose cord is not cut and who is not washed, salted, or swaddled. This negative picture makes bodily care of a weak infant the test case for the mercy and household nurture developed in the commentary.

basis: God sees the exposed infant and commands life
note: God passes the infant abandoned in blood and says, "Live." The rescue turns compassion toward a helpless child into decisive action, directly illuminating the commentary's definition of mercy as beneficence toward the weak.

basis: rescued infant grows to mature bodily fullness
note: In the continuing infant allegory, God causes the child to grow and arrive at maturity. The verse supplies a disturbing but precise prophetic instance of growth from exposure toward fullness, making the commentary's state-by-state completion image less sentimental.

basis: Abraham directs children and household in God's way
note: God's election of Abraham is tied to his commanding his children and household after him to keep YHWH's way. It puts religious formation inside the house, as the commentary puts nurture and teaching inside a family setting.

basis: kinship made through joined life
note: The commentary explains “rahim” kinship as relatives who came from one womb; Genesis gives a different foundation for family relation, saying husband and wife become one flesh, adding a bond formed through shared life rather than birth.

basis: a mother and child expelled from home
note: The commentary presents the home as the child’s place of nurture and protection; Sarah demands Hagar and her son be sent away, showing the contrary case of a household withdrawing that shelter.

basis: he child heard in distress
note: The commentary says mercy especially bends toward the weak and tells of Moses exposed by the river; in Hagar and Ishmael’s wilderness exile, God hears the boy crying and answers the vulnerable child.

basis: water for an abandoned child
note: The commentary connects nurturing to a child’s need for a sustaining home; God opens Hagar’s eyes to a well, and she gives the boy water after their household has been expelled.

basis: weaning marks a changed stage
note: The commentary describes raising a child from state to state; Abraham’s feast on the day Isaac is weaned marks the end of nursing and a public transition in the child’s life.

basis: two opposed peoples issue from one womb
note: God tells Rebekah that two nations and divided peoples are in her womb. It qualifies the commentary's association of one womb with kinship by showing a biblical womb that contains rivalry and eventual separation.

basis: pain in conception and childbirth
note: The verse makes painful childbearing part of Eve's condition. It is the direct biblical analogue for the commentary's insistence that the womb-house has a bodily cost after birth, even though its narrative frame is different.

basis: child borne on Rachel’s knees
note: The commentary notes a caregiver or step-parent raising a child beyond the birth mother; Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob so a child may be “borne upon my knees,” a maternal role formed through another woman’s birth.

basis: tender children and nursing flocks require a slow pace
note: Jacob refuses to drive on too hard because the children are tender and the flocks and herds are nursing. The verse unusually joins vulnerable children, lactating animals, and measured care, meeting the commentary's child and milk-sheep imagery.

basis: the cost of childbirth
note: The commentary records a female camel’s womb pain after giving birth; Rachel dies after childbirth and names her son in her final moments, showing the physical cost that the womb image can conceal.

basis: raḥamim / kin from one womb
note: The commentary explains kinship as “rahim,” relatives from one womb; Joseph’s raḥamim surge for Benjamin, his full brother by Rachel, when he sees him.

basis: source ر ح م: brotherly compassion, רחמים
note: Joseph's compassion for his brother is stirred so strongly that he must withdraw and weep. The Hebrew r-ḥ-m vocabulary lets the commentary's womb-derived kinship become a specific fraternal affect, without claiming that the two narratives are the same.

basis: Joseph provides for the household
note: The commentary notes the provision of food as one of the household images carried by the Arabic word-family; Joseph sustains his father, brothers, and their household with bread according to each family’s dependents.

basis: Jacob adopts Joseph’s sons
note: The commentary describes a spouse taking up the upbringing of the other spouse’s child; Jacob adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, giving them the standing of his first sons.

basis: blessings of breasts and womb
note: Jacob's blessing names the breasts and womb among God's life-giving blessings. It is a concentrated biblical counterpart to the commentary's paired attention to womb, birth, and milk-giving nurture.

basis: Joseph provides for kin and their little ones
note: Joseph promises to provide for his brothers and their little ones, then comforts them. It makes familial mercy material through food and reassurance, closely fitting the commentary's provisions-in-the-house and mercy-as-beneficence claims.

basis: Lo-Ruhamah, the child named Not-Compassionated
note: Hosea's daughter is named Lo-Ruhamah because God announces a withdrawal of r-ḥ-m compassion. Its negative naming makes the repeated Qur'anic merciful names more consequential: mercy can be represented as a relation to a child that is withheld as well as bestowed.

basis: Israel loved as a child and called out of Egypt
note: The commentary recounts Moses’ threatened infancy and return to his mother; Hosea depicts Israel collectively as God’s child, loved and called out of Egypt, turning the Exodus setting into a parent-child relation.

basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk
note: The commentary defines Rab as raising a child through successive stages; Hosea says God taught Ephraim to walk and took the child by the arms, presenting divine care as hands-on early nurture.

basis: loving bonds and feeding
note: The commentary links mercy with beneficence and raising a child toward completion; Hosea says God led Israel with loving bonds, bent down, and fed them. The middle image is rendered either as lifting an infant to the cheek or lifting a yoke from the jaws, so both readings remain visible.

basis: Ruhamah restored by divine mercy
note: The restoration oracle says that God will show r-ḥ-m compassion to Lo-Ruhamah and restore a belonging relation. Read after Hos. 1:6, it gives a narrative reversal of estrangement into parental mercy relevant to the commentary's merciful enclosing frame.

basis: a household official becomes a father to inhabitants
note: Eliakim receives office and is called a father to Jerusalem's inhabitants and Judah's house. It translates the commentary's qawwam image of one who upholds a household into public stewardship with explicitly parental language.

basis: instruction in successive measures
note: The commentary defines nurture as moving from state to state toward completion; Isaiah’s repeated “line upon line” formula pictures instruction in small, successive measures, though the verse’s tone may be satirical.

basis: weaned children as learners
note: The commentary says a teacher feeds people the small portions of knowledge; Isaiah asks whether the lesson is for the weaned and those just taken from the breast, using childhood feeding to frame instruction.

basis: shepherd carries lambs and leads nursing ewes
note: The commentary describes the home as a place of protection and sustenance; Isaiah pictures God gathering lambs in his arms, carrying them close, and gently leading nursing mothers.

basis: shepherd gathers lambs and gently leads mothers
note: The shepherd gathers lambs in his arms, carries them at his breast, and gently leads ewes with young. This joins weak young, maternal animals, and a caregiver's measured pace, supplying a pastoral analogue to the commentary's child and lactating-sheep images.

basis: carried from the womb onward
note: The commentary frames care as beginning in the womb and continuing through growth; Isaiah says God has carried Israel from the womb, extending the image from birth into a people’s long life.

basis: God carries people from belly and womb
note: God addresses those borne from the belly and carried from the womb. The parent-like divine carrying extends the commentary's home-to-maturity image beyond gestation into sustained care.

basis: care through old age
note: The commentary depicts nurture continuing toward completion; Isaiah promises to carry Israel even to old age and gray hairs, extending womb care across the whole life course.

basis: r-ḥ-m / womb and compassion
note: The commentary explicitly links Arabic raḥma to the womb; Isaiah uses Hebrew r-ḥ-m in a question about a mother forgetting the child of her womb, then says God will not forget Zion.

basis: mother’s care and divine mercy
note: The commentary frames the womb as a child’s home and mercy as care that acts; Isaiah asks whether a nursing mother can forget her child, then makes God’s unfailing remembrance exceed that maternal bond.

basis: source ر ح م: Hebrew רחם/רחמים, nursing mother
note: The Hebrew r-ḥ-m root supplies the verb for a mother's compassion while the verse speaks of her nursing child and the son of her belly. It is a close Semitic witness to the commentary's womb-to-mercy movement, then extends it to God's unfailing remembrance.

basis: foster fathers and nursing mothers
note: The commentary’s Rab/Râbbe image includes a non-birth parent raising a child; Isaiah imagines kings as foster fathers and queens as nursing mothers to Zion, extending household care to a restored people.

basis: foster fathers and nursing mothers
note: Kings are promised as foster fathers and queens as nursing mothers. This explicit pairing of adoptive authority and lactation provides a biblical counterpart to the commentary's nonbirth parent and child-minder senses of the r-b-b family.

basis: children taught by YHWH
note: All of Zion's children are described as taught by YHWH. The verse directly accompanies the commentary's Rahman who teaches and its extension of rabb into the teacher who feeds learners with small portions of knowledge.

basis: food and shelter for the vulnerable
note: The commentary defines mercy as tenderness that requires beneficence, especially for the weak, and notes a household’s provisions; Isaiah joins sharing bread with the hungry to bringing the homeless poor into one’s house and clothing the naked.

basis: children nursed, carried, and comforted
note: The commentary links the womb to a child’s home and later nurture; Isaiah depicts Jerusalem’s children nursing, being carried on her hip, and bounced on her knees, giving several concrete stages of maternal care.

basis: mother comforts a child
note: The commentary describes rahma as tenderness that becomes care; Isaiah compares God’s comfort of Jerusalem to a mother comforting her child, making maternal affection the measure of divine care.

basis: God brings to birth and does not shut the womb
note: God asks whether the one who brings to birth would fail to cause delivery or shut the womb. It gives a prophetic divine-birth image that directly accompanies the commentary's womb as a place governed by God.

basis: God forms and knows the prophet before birth
note: God says that he formed Jeremiah in the womb and knew him before he came out of it. This gives a biblical instance of prenatal divine formation that develops the commentary's claim that the womb is God's workshop.

basis: raḥem / compassion for Ephraim
note: The commentary labels Arabic ر ح م as mercy; the cognate Hebrew verb appears as God’s compassion for Ephraim, whom the verse calls a dear son and child, linking mercy with parental attachment.

basis: source ر ح م: divine compassion for a remembered son
note: Ephraim is called God's dear child; divine inward yearning culminates in the emphatic r-ḥ-m promise of mercy. The verse joins father-son relation and womb-derived compassion, sharpening the commentary's family account of rahma.

basis: gestation figured as milk being poured and curdled
note: Job describes his bodily beginning through liquid and milk-curdling imagery before the later clothing of flesh. Its deliberately domestic, embodied account of gestation belongs beside the commentary's womb as vessel and its lactating-animal image.

basis: birth as a wished-for escape
note: The commentary presents the womb as the child’s first home; Job asks why he did not die at birth, giving a contrary view in which womb and birth do not guarantee a secure or merciful life.

basis: knees and breasts as early care
note: The commentary moves from the womb to a child’s home and nourishment; Job asks why knees received him and why breasts nursed him, naming the post-birth acts that the commentary gathers into the image of nurture.

basis: one Maker fashions persons in the womb
note: Job grounds his refusal to oppress servants in the fact that the same Maker formed both parties in the womb. It turns shared prenatal origin into an ethical relation, illuminating the commentary's move from one womb to kinship and mercy for the vulnerable.

basis: compassionate mothers reversed by famine
note: In siege, women called compassionate cook their own children for food. This horrific reversal makes maternal compassion and household nourishment collapse into their opposites, a counter-image to the commentary's merciful womb-home.

basis: nursing father carries a child
note: The commentary’s “Rab” image is a non-birth parent who raises a child; Moses asks whether he conceived or gave birth to Israel and must carry them “as a nurse carries a suckling,” voicing the burden of foster care.

basis: a nurse carries a suckling
note: The commentary’s image of the foster parent is explicitly about taking charge of a child one did not give birth to; Moses uses the nurse carrying a suckling to describe being made responsible for a people he did not conceive.

basis: nurse carries a suckling child
note: Moses protests that he did not conceive or bear Israel and so cannot carry them as a nurse carries a suckling child. The verse is a precise nonbiological-caregiver analogy for the commentary's rabb/rabba and nurse who undertake a child's nurture.

basis: jealousy within a suspected marriage
note: A husband's spirit of jealousy arises in the ordeal for a wife suspected of infidelity. It is a concrete biblical household setting for the commentary's secondary gayrah image of guarding family, but its suspicion and legal ordeal complicate any simple protective reading.

basis: discipline as parental care
note: The commentary portrays raising a child as purposeful formation; Proverbs connects a parent’s love with diligent correction, a sharper form of nurture than the commentary’s gentler household image.

basis: train a child in a way
note: The commentary defines tarbiya as bringing a thing through stages toward completion; Proverbs tells an adult to train a child in the way he should go, relating instruction to the child’s later life.

basis: train a child in the way to go
note: The proverb explicitly speaks of training a child for his way so that age will not make him depart from it. It is a concise Hebrew Bible formulation of the commentary's terbiye as directed, enduring formation.

basis: q-w-m is not the link; parental discipline is
note: The commentary defines Rab as raising a child toward completion; Proverbs says the Lord corrects the one he loves as a father corrects a son, supplying a direct Hebrew parental-formation motif.

basis: source ن ع م: Hebrew נעם, pleasant paths
note: Wisdom's ways are called ways of pleasantness and her paths peace. Hebrew n-ʿ-m is cognate with the source en'amte family, but the biblical verse applies pleasantness to wisdom's path rather than importing the commentary's child-rearing sense.

basis: food apportioned to the household
note: The capable woman rises at night to give food to her household and portions to her servants. It realizes the commentary's secondary image of provisions brought into a home as an act that keeps its members alive.

basis: care of the household
note: The commentary’s household upholder is one who keeps the family’s affairs standing; the capable woman watches the ways of her household and is not idle, a concrete domestic stewardship image.

basis: q-w-m / children rise in the household
note: The commentary labels Arabic ق و م for the one who keeps household affairs standing; Hebrew qûm is a cognate used when the woman’s children rise to call her blessed, placing the root in a household where her care is recognized.

basis: father teaches a tender child
note: The commentary’s “Rab” is one who raises a child and its teacher nourishes learners; Proverbs recalls being a tender child, uniquely loved by his mother, while his father taught him.

basis: parental instruction toward life
note: The commentary describes upbringing as progressive formation; the father’s instruction tells the child to hold fast to the words and live, giving a concrete parental lesson aimed at mature conduct.

basis: source ر ح م: fatherly compassion for children
note: The psalm compares YHWH's compassion for those who fear him to a father's compassion for children, using the r-ḥ-m root. It gives a paternal rendering of the commentary's Rahman/Rahim frame around nurturing lordship.

basis: fatherly raḥamim
note: The commentary’s Arabic mercy root corresponds to Hebrew r-ḥ-m in a verse comparing God’s compassion to a father’s compassion for children, giving the lexical link a concrete parental setting.

basis: father and children
note: The commentary’s womb-to-parental-care frame meets the psalm’s explicit image of God’s compassion like a father’s for children; it interprets mercy as a sustained relation, not an abstract quality.

basis: children as fruit of the womb
note: The commentary begins its frame with the womb as the child’s home; the psalm calls children an inheritance from God and the fruit of the womb a reward, assigning value to the life that grows there.

basis: quieted soul like a weaned child with its mother
note: The psalm compares its quieted soul to a weaned child with its mother. It adds the post-nursing stage of peaceful attachment to the commentary's womb, breast, and gradual completion sequence.

basis: a weaned child with its mother
note: The commentary describes a child’s growth inside a home and the transition toward completion; the psalm compares its quieted soul to a weaned child beside its mother, where dependence has changed but maternal closeness remains.

basis: n-ʿ-m / pleasant kinship
note: The commentary labels Arabic ن ع م and glosses it with raising children in comfort; Hebrew naʿim is a cognate meaning pleasant, used here of brothers dwelling together, so the source’s comfort image meets a concrete kin household.

basis: God forms within the mother's womb
note: The psalm credits God with forming the inward parts and weaving the speaker in the mother's womb. It directly accompanies the commentary's Qur'an 3:6 image of God shaping a person in the rahim as a place of formation.

basis: formed in the mother’s womb
note: The commentary makes the womb a place where a child grows and is formed; the psalm says God knit the speaker together in his mother’s womb, locating divine making within that home.

basis: womb and mother’s breasts
note: The commentary calls the womb a child’s first home and describes subsequent nurture; the psalmist says God took him from the womb and made him secure at his mother’s breasts.

basis: God brings the speaker from womb to mother's breasts
note: The speaker credits God with drawing him from the womb and making him trust at his mother's breasts. It holds together God's hidden guardianship and maternal nourishment, the two agents the commentary distinguishes in Musa's infancy.

basis: cast from the womb toward God
note: The commentary’s womb image is a home for the child; the psalm says the speaker was cast upon God from birth and relied on God from his mother’s womb, extending the image from maternal shelter to divine care.

basis: God receives the one abandoned by parents
note: Even if father and mother forsake the speaker, YHWH receives him. It provides a compact divine-foster-parent image beside the commentary's insistence that the one who truly raises a child may be other than the visible household.

basis: God instructs with an eye upon the learner
note: God promises to instruct and teach the way to go, counsel the speaker, and keep an eye upon him. It closely matches the commentary's conjunction of teaching and Musa being raised under God's eye.

basis: father of orphans and defender of widows
note: The commentary’s household upholder is responsible for the family, and mercy especially reaches the weak; the psalm calls God father of orphans and defender of widows.

basis: solitary people settled in a home
note: The commentary’s central image is a household that shelters and raises a child; the next Hebrew verse says God settles the solitary in a home.

basis: God supports from the womb
note: The commentary pictures mercy as care that begins in the womb and continues through a child’s growth; the psalmist says he has leaned on God from birth and was taken from the womb by God.

basis: Naomi becomes the child’s nurse
note: The commentary’s rabîbe gloss is a caretaker of a child; Naomi takes the newborn into her lap and becomes his nurse, making a non-birth grandmother the child’s caregiver.

basis: Naomi holds the child and becomes his nurse
note: Naomi takes the newborn to her bosom and becomes his nurse. The scene makes kinship, bodily closeness, and an elder woman's nonmaternal nurture converge in the way the commentary's womb-derived family language invites.

basis: God’s spirit sustains and teaches
note: The commentary links the merciful Lord with the teacher who raises people gradually; Wisdom says God’s imperishable spirit is in all things, directly joining divine presence with sustained life.

basis: gradual correction toward maturity
note: The commentary defines tarbiya as bringing something state by state to completion; Wisdom says God corrects offenders little by little so they may abandon evil and trust him.

basis: common formation in a mother's womb
note: The speaker says that he was molded in flesh in a mother's womb and had the same entrance into life as all others. This Jewish reflection turns prenatal formation into common human kinship, echoing the commentary's one-womb logic.
